title: Sell Mineral Rights in Midwest, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Midwest, WY
metaDescription: Own minerals near the old Salt Creek company town of Midwest? Get an offer priced against real stripper-well production, not a guess.
heroLead: Midwest, Wyoming was built as a company town for the Salt Creek field, and the name says exactly what the town was for. If your minerals sit here, they almost certainly trace to that old field.
intro: Midwest sits right in the old Salt Creek oil field in Natrona County, one of the earliest big fields discovered in Wyoming and still producing today off shallow stripper wells on artificial lift. The town itself was built by the oil companies that ran the field, and most mineral ownership around here traces back to homestead-era interests carved up through inheritance over the last hundred-plus years.

sections.heading: A field that has been paying royalty for a century
paragraphs: Salt Creek's decline curve flattened out long ago. The wells around Midwest are stripper production now, low volume but steady, and that steadiness is actually useful for pricing your interest — a buyer does not have to guess where the curve is headed because it has been in roughly the same place for years. Most of the artificial lift equipment on these wells has been swapped out and rebuilt more than once, but the underlying reservoir behavior has stayed consistent.

sections.heading: Small fractional interests are normal here
paragraphs: Because this ground has been producing so long, original interests have split through two, three, sometimes four generations of heirs. If your share is a sixteenth or smaller of a Salt Creek tract, that is common and not a problem — we buy exactly the fraction you own, not a bigger piece.

sections.heading: What to have ready
paragraphs: A recent division order or check stub with your decimal interest and the well or unit name gets a Midwest file moving fastest. If all you have is an old lease or a probate document naming your share, send that and we can trace it through Natrona County clerk records.

faqs.question: Is a Salt Creek stripper-well royalty even worth selling?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. Stable, long-running stripper production is one of the easier interests to price fairly because the decline is already known.

faqs.question: My share is small — a sixteenth or less. Do you still buy that?
faqs.answer: Yes. Small fractional interests from long-held family land are common around Midwest and we buy them regularly.

faqs.question: What if I don't have a current division order?
faqs.answer: Send us whatever you have — old lease, deed, or probate paperwork — and we'll trace your interest through the courthouse records in Casper.

faqs.question: How long has Salt Creek been producing?
faqs.answer: Over a century. It was one of the earliest major fields discovered in Wyoming, and the long, well-documented decline is part of what makes interests here easier to price fairly.
